title: The ChatGPT landscape: models, features, and plans

opening.headline: On the ChatGPT screen, the model, function, and plan name appear all at once. Learn how to read these names by dividing them into layers.
body: When using ChatGPT, you encounter model names starting with GPT, function names such as Search or Deep research, and plan names such as Free or Plus on one screen. They are all clustered around 'ChatGPT', so it's easy to get confused about which name refers to what.

In this class, you will learn how to break your name down into five layers: company, model, product, features, and plan. Next, let's check which layers the ChatGPT feature overview document and model release notes cover, and classify the news that a 'new model has been released' into layers.
objectives: You can distinguish between company, model, product, function, and plan layers.
You can classify items by floor in the ChatGPT function overview
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

screens.title: Names mixed on one screen
screens.lead:
Let's look at three types of names commonly encountered on the ChatGPT screen. When you select each item, an explanation will unfold.

The GPT-5.6 Sol case in this lesson is a release case that explains the differences in models, products, and plans at the time. Please do not read this as the latest basic model list, but check the available models and administrator settings for each Chat·Work·Codex separately as of 2026-10.

visual.alt: Model screen with model selection menu, tool menu, and rate plan information all on one screen

items.prompt: What names do you see in the model selection menu?
items.answer: Several GPT family names are listed. This name refers to the engine that produces the answer, or model. Paid plans allow you to choose between several base models, the feature overview document explains.

items.prompt: What names do you see in the Tools menu?
items.answer: You'll see names like Search (web search), Deep research, and image input and creation. These names refer to tools or functions that can be turned on and used within ChatGPT. The feature overview document reveals that the available tools vary depending on your subscription level and settings.

items.prompt: What name does I see in the plan information?
items.answer: You'll see subscription level names like Free and Go. This name refers to the plan, and the same model or feature may or may not be visible depending on the plan.

Each name is not difficult. Because the names of different layers are mixed on one screen, it is difficult to tell which name is the model, which name is the function, and which name is the plan. Splitting names into tiers greatly reduces this confusion.

screens.outro: First, let me think about how much I know about the name I use.

screens.title: Remember: How many names do I know?
screens.lead: Read the questions and think for yourself first. You do not enter or submit answers; simply select an item and the instructor's thoughts will unfold.

items.prompt: How many of the features you currently use in ChatGPT do you know the exact names of?
items.answer: Most people use vague names like ‘that button’ or ‘that mode’ rather than knowing the exact name. That too is natural. You can write without knowing the name, but you'll need the correct name when reading news or talking to your team.

items.prompt: Is that the model name, feature name, or plan name?
items.answer: If you break it down lightly, 'turn on search' is a function, 'name starting with GPT' is a model, and 'change to paid' is a plan. There are many cases where the three layers are mixed within one sentence. This class provides a framework for unpacking that mix.

items.prompt: What do you check first when you hear new news?
items.answer: Usually, I start by checking, ‘Does it appear on my screen?’ The confirmation actually depends on which level of change the news is about. If there is a change in the model, you should look at the model selection menu, if there is a change in function, you should look at the tools menu, and if there is a change in plan, you should look at your subscription level.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the framework for dividing names into five tiers.

screens.title: Five layers: company, model, product, function, plan
screens.lead: The next steps break down the names into five layers. Select the next arrow to stack the layers one by one. You can go back to the previous arrow and see it again.

visual.alt: Five-layer diagram with companies, models, products, features, and plans stacked vertically
labels: Company: A place that creates services
Model: The engine that generates the answer
View all five floors at a glance

steps.title: Company: A place that creates services
steps.body: The top layer is the company that creates the service. ChatGPT is created by OpenAI. You can think of the company name separately from the name of the product or model. The sentence ‘OpenAI announced’ does not tell you which layer has changed, so you must identify the layer by looking at the name that follows it.

steps.title: Model: The engine that generates the answer
steps.body: A model is an AI engine that receives questions and creates answers. The feature overview document explains that users on paid plans can choose from several base models. Names like GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.4 mini belong to this layer. Models are more like interchangeable parts within the same dialog window.

steps.title: Product: Human entrance
steps.body: Products are the gateway where people meet services. ChatGPT and Codex are different products. In model release notes, news about one model may be written across ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex. This is because the same model is used in multiple products.

steps.title: Function: Tools within the product
steps.body: Functions are tools that can be turned on and used within the product. The feature overview document lists Search (web search), deep research, image input and creation, file and audio upload, data analysis, voice mode, Canvas, memory, projects, scheduled tasks, and custom GPT. The documentation adds that the tools you use will vary depending on your subscription level and settings.

steps.title: Plan: Who Writes What
steps.body: Plans are at the subscription level. The same models and features may or may not be visible depending on the plan. For example, GPT-5.6 Sol is available sequentially on eligible paid plans, Free and Go, and does not include non-logged-in users. The plan is the layer that determines whether you can use it on your screen.

steps.title: View all five floors at a glance
steps.body: To summarize, the company is where it was made, the model is the engine, the product is the entrance, the function is the tool, and the plan is the terms of use. When we come across a name, we first ask ‘which floor is this?’ and then check its relationship with other floors. This one question will give you direction in the flood of names on the screen.

screens.outro: Now that we have the layers, let's take a look at how the actual help document contains these layers.

screens.title: How to read the feature overview and release notes
screens.lead: The following article is an excerpt from the model release notes. When you select an underlined phrase, you will see which layer it is named for and why.

visual.alt: Mockup with feature overview document and model release notes side-by-side and color coded for each layer

data.text: Introducing GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT. GPT-5.6 Sol is rolling out to eligible paid ChatGPT plans. Free, Go, and logged-out users are not included. Availability may vary during rollout, and managed-workspace access can depend on administrator settings.

marks.note: Name of the model layer. This means that a new engine for generating answers has been released, but it does not mean that new features have been created.
This is the product layer. This news informs you that the change will be applied at the entrance called ChatGPT.
These are the conditions of the plan floor. This means it's only available on eligible paid plans, so you'll need to check your subscription level as well.

marks.span: Free, Go, and logged-out users are not included
marks.note: This is a sentence that identifies what is excluded from the plan layer. This model will not be visible on the user's screen.

marks.span: managed-workspace access can depend on administrator settings
marks.note: This is a condition based on settings. In organization-managed workspaces, access may vary depending on administrator settings.

screens.outro: Now that you have learned the reading order, let's move on to an example of classifying a piece of news yourself.

screens.title: Commentary example: News that ‘a new model has been released’
screens.lead: The instructor shows the process of classifying the news that 'a new model has been released' into layers. Select the next arrow and follow the solution step by step.

steps.title: Read the news as it is
steps.body: The news of the case is as follows. 'OpenAI has started providing the new model GPT-5.6 Sol on ChatGPT.' This sentence contains the company, model, and product name all at once. The first judgment is ‘what does this news change?’ If you read the sentence and immediately accept that ‘my ChatGPT will change’, you have not differentiated between layers.

steps.title: Step 1: Find the floor the name refers to
steps.body: GPT-5.6 Sol is the model name. The release notes also introduce this model as the flagship inference model for complex tasks. So this news is not a new feature, but a change in the model layer. ChatGPT is the product layer that serves as the entrance, and OpenAI is the company layer.

steps.title: Step 2: Read our offerings
steps.body: Next, read the scope of offer. The release notes say it's rolling out to eligible paid plans and doesn't include Free, Go, or non-logged-in users. In other words, it is a change with conditions attached to the plan layer. Even if there is news about the same model, the results on my screen will be different if the plans are different.

steps.title: Step 3: Check settings and timing
steps.body: The document adds that availability may vary during rollout, and in managed workspaces, access may vary depending on administrator settings. Therefore, the screen may be different even from colleagues using the same plan. In this case, it's important to understand that the 'delivering sequence' statement itself is a normal state.

steps.title: Step 4: Decide where to check on your screen
steps.body: Since this is a change in the model layer, the confirmation point is the model selection menu. Opening the Tools menu does not show the new model. If you don't see it in the menu, first check whether your plan is eligible for this offer and, if it's an organizational account, what the administrator settings are.

steps.title: Compare feature news
steps.body: For comparison, let's consider a piece of feature news. If it is news that 'Deep research can now be used in ChatGPT', the layer that the name refers to is a function. In this case, the checkpoint is the Tools menu, not the model selection menu, and the scope of offers must also be read separately based on subscription level and settings. The point of this example is that even if it is the same ‘new news’, the place to check it is different depending on the floor.

steps.title: Step 5: Write a Conclusion
steps.body: The conclusion is summarized in two lines. First, this news is a change in the model layer and not a new feature. Second, what you see on your screen is determined by your plan and settings. In the same way, you can also read the news that ‘model is retiring’. The release notes state that GPT-5.5 has been retired from ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex, but API access is not affected, and this also reveals changes in the model layer along with product-specific scope.

screens.outro: Now that we have analyzed one piece of news in layers, we will organize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Summary: more layers than names
screens.lead: Let's summarize what we've seen so far. Read slowly and think about which layer to place the functions you use.

paragraphs: Separating the five layers of company, model, product, features, and plan reduces confusion about having the same word 'ChatGPT' used across multiple layers. The key is to get into the habit of asking ‘which floor is this?’ instead of memorizing the name.

The ChatGPT feature overview is a document that compiles the items of the feature layer, and the model release notes are a document that organizes the releases, updates, and retirements of the model layer in date order. Both articles tell me that my screen may vary depending on my subscription level and settings.
When I come across new news, I first classify which floor the change is for, read what plan it covers, and then decide where to check it on my screen.

This method can also be used outside of ChatGPT. When you come across a new name for any service, the conversation will be much more accurate if you ask where it was created, the engine, the entrance, the tools, or the terms of use. Even when you say to a team member, ‘I don’t see that function,’ if you tell them the name of which floor it is, it will take less time to find the cause.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: You can understand the same news much faster if you read it in layers. Even if the model changes or is retired, it is written in each news whether the impact is limited to ChatGPT or also affects the API. Read the scope together. Lastly, the release notes include not only releases but also updates, retirements, and model spec changes, so it is a good idea to look at the title of each item and start reading to determine what type of news it is.

glossary.def: It is an AI engine that generates answers. This is the tier selected within the product, and paid plans allow you to choose from several base models.
It is the entrance where people meet services. ChatGPT and Codex are different products.
It is a tool that can be turned on and used within the product. Search, deep research, image creation, memory, etc.
Subscription level. Even with the same product, the available models and features vary depending on the plan.
A document that records a model's release, update, and retirement with dates.

misconceptions.myth: If you know the model name, you know everything about ChatGPT.
misconceptions.fact: The model is just one of the five floors. You need to check separately what features can be used and which plan they are available on.

misconceptions.myth: Since a new model has been released, it will appear on my screen right away.
misconceptions.fact: The new model will roll out to eligible plans in stages, and will also affect admin settings for organizational accounts. Even if the news comes out, it may not be on your screen yet.

misconceptions.myth: Search and Deep research are the same function with different names.
misconceptions.fact: The two are different functions. Search is a web search for up-to-date information, and deep research is a multi-step research function that reads and synthesizes multiple sources to produce structured results with citations.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The name can be divided into five layers: company, model, product, feature, and plan.
A feature overview is a list of feature layers, and release notes are a record of changes in model layers.
After classifying which floor the new news is, I look at the scope of coverage and the confirmation points on my screen.
Sorting by layer rather than name reduces confusion.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where are the three functions I use in ChatGPT placed on each of the five layers?

checks.q: Match the following names with the floor they belong to
right: Product Layer: A different entrance from ChatGPT
Company layer: Where services are created
Functional layer: Web search tools within the product
Model Layer: The Engine That Creates the Answer
checks.explain: Companies, models, products, features, and plans are different layers. Even if they are gathered near the same ChatGPT, each name belongs to only one layer.
checks.intro: The names around ChatGPT have different levels. Match the names and floors.
checks.correctFeedback: All are correct. You have correctly identified the five layers: company, model, product, features, and plan.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Each name belongs to only one layer. Divide it into the place that creates the service, the engine that creates the answer, the entrance, the tool, and the subscription level.

checks.q: What is the best interpretation of the news that 'the new model will be offered sequentially to eligible paid plans and Free will not be included'?
options: A new feature is coming and will appear on every user's screen right away
The plan determines whether it is a change in the model floor and whether it is visible on my screen.
The plan name has changed, but the model has not changed.
Because it is a change in the product layer, it only applies to Codex users.
checks.explain: The floor the name refers to is the model, and the scope of provision is subject to plan conditions. So the point to check is whether it is visible in the model selection menu.

wrong.0: It is not immediately visible to all users, but is provided sequentially depending on the plan.
wrong.2: Since it is news that a new model has been released, it is a change in the model layer.
wrong.3: A model is an engine layer, not a product, and this is not news specific to Codex.

checks.intro: When reading news, it is important to know which level the change is in. Choose the appropriate interpretation.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. It is a change in the model floor, and whether it is visible on your screen is determined by the plan conditions, so you can check it in the model selection menu.
checks.incorrectFeedback: News of a new model should not be read as immediately adding features for all users. Please look at the floor the name refers to and the plan conditions separately.
